body.en: Everything so far has lived inside \( \mathbb{R}^n \). This chapter names the handful of properties that made all of it work — closure under addition and scalar multiplication, the existence of a zero vector — as the axioms of a vector space, then asks which subsets of a vector space are themselves vector spaces (subspaces), and how few vectors it takes to reach every point in one (span, linear independence, basis, dimension).

A vector space \( V \) over \( \mathbb{R} \) is a set with an addition and a scalar multiplication satisfying: closure (\( \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in V \), \( c\mathbf{u}\in V \)), commutativity and associativity of addition, a zero vector \( \mathbf{0} \) with \( \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{v} \), an additive inverse \( -\mathbf{v} \) for every \( \mathbf{v} \), and the distributive/associative laws linking scalars and addition. \( \mathbb{R}^n \) (Chapter 1) is the running example, but the same axioms are satisfied by the set of all polynomials of degree \( \le n \), by \( m\times n \) matrices under matrix addition, and by continuous functions on an interval — every fact proved in this chapter from the axioms alone applies to all of them at once.

A subset \( W\subseteq V \) of a vector space is a subspace if \( W \) is itself a vector space under \( V \)'s addition and scalar multiplication — equivalently (Theorem 5.1 below), if \( W \) is closed under those two operations and contains \( \mathbf{0} \).

A nonempty subset \( W\subseteq V \) is a subspace if and only if it satisfies all three: (1) \( \mathbf{0}\in W \); (2) \( \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in W\Rightarrow\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in W \); (3) \( \mathbf{u}\in W,\,c\in\mathbb{R}\Rightarrow c\mathbf{u}\in W \).

(\( \Rightarrow \)) If \( W \) is a subspace, it is a vector space in its own right, so it has a zero vector and is closed under both operations by Definition 5.1 — giving (1)–(3) directly.

(\( \Leftarrow \)) Suppose \( W \) satisfies (1)–(3). Every axiom of Definition 5.1 that is an equation holding for all vectors in \( V \) — commutativity, associativity, the distributive laws — automatically holds for the vectors of \( W \) too, since they are still vectors of \( V \). What remains is exactly closure (guaranteed by (2), (3)), the zero vector (guaranteed by (1)), and additive inverses: for \( \mathbf{v}\in W \), condition (3) with \( c=-1 \) gives \( -\mathbf{v}=(-1)\mathbf{v}\in W \). So \( W \) satisfies every axiom of Definition 5.1 and is itself a vector space.

label.en: Worked example 5.A — Applying the subspace test

body.en:
Is \( W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3 : x+2y-z=0\} \) a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^3 \)?

\( \mathbf{0}=(0,0,0) \) satisfies \( 0+0-0=0 \), so (1) holds. If \( \mathbf{u}=(x_1,y_1,z_1) \), \( \mathbf{v}=(x_2,y_2,z_2)\in W \), then \( (x_1+x_2)+2(y_1+y_2)-(z_1+z_2)=(x_1+2y_1-z_1)+(x_2+2y_2-z_2)=0+0=0 \), so \( \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in W \) — (2) holds. Similarly \( cx_1+2(cy_1)-cz_1=c(x_1+2y_1-z_1)=0 \), so (3) holds. All three conditions hold: \( W \) is a subspace (geometrically, a plane through the origin).

By contrast, \( U=\{(x,y,z):x+2y-z=1\} \) fails (1) immediately — \( \mathbf{0} \) gives \( 0\neq1 \) — so \( U \) is not a subspace (it's a plane that misses the origin).

A linear combination of vectors \( \mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k \) is any vector \( c_1\mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf{v}_k \) for scalars \( c_i\in\mathbb{R} \). Their span, \( \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k) \), is the set of all such linear combinations. The span of any set of vectors is automatically a subspace — closure under addition and scaling is immediate from the definition, and \( \mathbf{0} \) is the linear combination with every \( c_i=0 \).

body.en: Vectors \( \mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k \) are linearly independent if the only solution of \[ c_1\mathbf{v}_1+c_2\mathbf{v}_2+\cdots+c_k\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0} \] is the trivial one, \( c_1=c_2=\cdots=c_k=0 \). If some other solution exists, the vectors are linearly dependent — equivalently, at least one \( \mathbf{v}_i \) is a linear combination of the others.

If \( \mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k \) are linearly independent and \( \mathbf{w}\in\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k) \), then \( \mathbf{w} \) is a linear combination of \( \mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k \) in exactly one way.

Existence is immediate: \( \mathbf{w}\in\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k) \) means, by Definition 5.3, that some linear combination equals \( \mathbf{w} \).

For uniqueness, suppose \( \mathbf{w}=c_1\mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf{v}_k=d_1\mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+d_k\mathbf{v}_k \) are two representations. Subtracting, \[ (c_1-d_1)\mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+(c_k-d_k)\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0}. \] Since \( \mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k \) are linearly independent, Definition 5.4 forces every coefficient to be \( 0 \): \( c_i-d_i=0 \), i.e. \( c_i=d_i \) for every \( i \). The two representations are identical.

Are \( \mathbf{v}_1=(1,2,0) \), \( \mathbf{v}_2=(0,1,1) \), \( \mathbf{v}_3=(2,1,-2) \) linearly independent?

Set \( c_1\mathbf{v}_1+c_2\mathbf{v}_2+c_3\mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{0} \): \( c_1+2c_3=0 \), \( 2c_1+c_2+c_3=0 \), \( c_2-2c_3=0 \).

From the first, \( c_1=-2c_3 \); from the third, \( c_2=2c_3 \). Substituting into the second: \( 2(-2c_3)+2c_3+c_3=-4c_3+2c_3+c_3=-c_3=0\Rightarrow c_3=0 \), forcing \( c_1=c_2=0 \) too.

Only the trivial solution exists: the three vectors are linearly independent.

A basis of a vector space \( V \) is a linearly independent set that spans \( V \). Every basis of a given \( V \) has the same number of vectors — that common number is the dimension of \( V \), \( \dim V \). By Theorem 5.2, once a basis is fixed, every vector of \( V \) has a unique representation as a linear combination of basis vectors — its coordinates. The standard basis of \( \mathbb{R}^n \) is \( \mathbf{e}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{e}_n \) (each \( \mathbf{e}_i \) has a \( 1 \) in position \( i \) and \( 0 \) elsewhere), so \( \dim\mathbb{R}^n=n \).

value.en: Linearly independent + spans \( V \); size \( =\dim V \)

body.en:
Let \( W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3 : x=2y\} \). (a) Show \( W \) is a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^3 \). (b) Find a basis for \( W \) and state \( \dim W \).

Show solution

(a) \( \mathbf{0}=(0,0,0) \) satisfies \( 0=2(0) \). If \( (x_1,y_1,z_1),(x_2,y_2,z_2)\in W \) then \( x_1+x_2=2y_1+2y_2=2(y_1+y_2) \), so the sum is in \( W \); similarly for scalar multiples. All three subspace-test conditions hold.

(b) Every vector of \( W \) has the form \( (2y,y,z)=y(2,1,0)+z(0,0,1) \), so \( \{(2,1,0),(0,0,1)\} \) spans \( W \); it's also linearly independent (neither is a scalar multiple of the other). Basis: \( \{(2,1,0),(0,0,1)\} \), \( \dim W=2 \).

Show that \( (1,1) \) and \( (1,-1) \) span \( \mathbb{R}^2 \).

Solution: Given any \( (a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2 \), solve \( c_1(1,1)+c_2(1,-1)=(a,b) \): \( c_1+c_2=a \), \( c_1-c_2=b \).

Adding and subtracting: \( c_1=\frac{a+b}{2} \), \( c_2=\frac{a-b}{2} \) — always solvable, so every \( (a,b) \) is reachable. They span \( \mathbb{R}^2 \).

Are \( (1,2,3) \), \( (2,4,6) \), \( (0,1,0) \) linearly independent?

Solution: \( (2,4,6)=2(1,2,3) \) — the second vector is a scalar multiple of the first.

Taking \( c_1=2,\,c_2=-1,\,c_3=0 \) gives \( 2(1,2,3)-1(2,4,6)+0(0,1,0)=\mathbf{0} \), a nontrivial solution. The set is linearly dependent.

question.en: Practice: Determine whether \( (1,0,1) \), \( (0,1,1) \), \( (1,1,1) \) form a basis for \( \mathbb{R}^3 \).

solution.en: Setting \( c_1(1,0,1)+c_2(0,1,1)+c_3(1,1,1)=\mathbf{0} \) gives \( c_1+c_3=0 \), \( c_2+c_3=0 \), \( c_1+c_2+c_3=0 \). Substituting \( c_1=-c_3,\,c_2=-c_3 \) into the third: \( -c_3-c_3+c_3=-c_3=0\Rightarrow c_3=0 \), so \( c_1=c_2=0 \) too — linearly independent. Three independent vectors in a 3-dimensional space automatically span it (Theorem 5.2's uniqueness plus a dimension-counting argument), so yes, they form a basis.
